A California Apple customer has filed a class-action lawsuit accusing the company of misleading customers into believing the privacy protections of the "Hide My Email" feature were real. Here's what's going on.

Apple Sued Over Hide My Email Flaw

Recently, 404 Media reported that Apple knew about a flaw — one that allegedly leaks the real email addresses behind Hide My Email aliases — for over a year.

Apple's Hide My Email feature lets users create unique, randomly generated email addresses that forward messages to their personal inbox, so they don't have to reveal their actual email when signing up for apps, websites, and newsletters.

It's available for free through Sign in with Apple, while a more robust version is included with an iCloud+ plan (starting at $0.99/month), letting users create aliases for websites, newsletters, and other services.

According to 404 Media, a security researcher warned Apple about the flaw back in June 2025, noting that it could expose the real email addresses behind Hide My Email aliases.

Apple acknowledged receiving the report roughly a month later, but reportedly never addressed the issue. In March 2026, the company claimed it had fixed the flaw, though the researcher found it remained exploitable.

As for the lawsuit itself (reported by MacRumors), plaintiff Anthony Alvarez says:

Apple knew about the problem for over a year and still hasn't fixed it — yet Apple continues to profit from Hide My Email and its privacy promises. Plaintiff is one of the millions of customers who paid for iCloud+ and trusted Apple's claim that Hide My Email would protect their personal email addresses. Plaintiff and the class paid Apple for privacy — iCloud+ users through a premium included in their iCloud+ subscription fee, and all Apple customers through a premium baked into the price of Apple products (which Apple packages as offering stronger privacy protections).

The lawsuit also claims this isn't an isolated incident, citing a 2023 report that Apple's randomized MAC address feature might leak users' real hardware identifiers.

It further notes that the aggregate class-member claims being advanced by the named plaintiff exceed $5 million (excluding interest and attorneys' fees), without explaining how that number was reached.

Alvarez is suing on behalf of himself and other Apple customers who claim to have been similarly affected. He's asking the court to certify the case as a class action covering four proposed user groups:

  • All nationwide Apple customers who purchased a device and used Hide My Email;
  • A California subset of those users;
  • All nationwide iCloud+ subscribers who used the feature;
  • A California subset of those iCloud+ subscribers.

He's asking for a jury trial and, in addition to monetary damages in an amount to be determined, he's asking the court to order Apple to fix Hide My Email or clearly disclose its limitations.

Apple has not yet responded to the lawsuit.

Let us know in the comments whether you think this class action should be certified.
